3. 
The Rulemaking Revolution: Judicial and Congressional, The 1960s 
and 1970s saw a dramatic increase in agency use of rulemaking. For some 
agencies, like the FTC in Petroleum Refiners, the increase depended on judicial 
decisions that interpreted old substantive statutes to confer rulemaking power 
over private conduct even though nobody had thought to interpret the statutes 
that way for decades beforehand. Another major example of such novel judicial 
interpretation involved the rulemaking authority of the Food and Drug 
Administration over matters like adulteration and branding under the Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938. After a favorable suggestion from the 
Supreme Court in Abbott Labs v. Gardner in 1967 (discussed in Chapter 8), a 
series of cases in the Second Circuit affirmed the FDA’s newly-expanded 
reinterpretation of its rulemaking powers. See Natl Nutritional Foods Ass'n v. 
Weinberger, 512 F.2d 688 (2d Cir. 1975); United States v. Nova Scotia Food 
Prods. Corp., 568 F.2d 240 (2d Cir. 1977); Natl, Ass’n of Pharm. Mfrs. v. FDA, 
637 F.2d 877 (2d Cir. 1981). A 1975 line from Judge Mansfield summarizes 
£
well the Second Circuit’s approach to statutory interpretation in these cases: 
“Where once we may have demanded proof of specific delegation of legislative 
authority to an agency purporting to promulgate substantive rules, we have 
learned from experience to accept a general delegation as sufficient in certain 
areas of expertise.” Natl Nutritional Foods Ass’n v. Weinberger, supra, 512 
F.2d at 696. 
«
But probably the more important driver of the rulemaking revolution was 
m
that Congress, enacting new substantive statutes in the 1960s and beyond, 
conferred rulemaking authority on agencies (especially ones like EPA, OSHA, 
and NHTSA) in explicit and specific language that left no need for creative 
interpretation of general provisions. Such authorizations are central to modem 
*
regulatory statutes up to the present era, as exemplified in the Affordable Care 
Act and Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, which each require numerous rulemakings.
Because of these many exphcit provisions, agency authority to promulgate 
rules has usually not been a contested issue.
When it comes to the very general grants of rulemaking authority that 
were construed so generously in Petroleum Refiners or in the FDA cases cited
